Pidyon ha-ben. The name means redemption of the firstborn, and it refers to a ceremony in which the parents of a firstborn son symbolically redeem him from priestly service by paying a sum to a kohen, a member of the Jewish priestly class. The ceremony takes place thirty days after the child's birth, or later if necessary, but never on Shabbat or a major holiday.

The ceremony is obligatory only for firstborn sons whose mother had not been previously married and whose father is not himself a kohen or levi, members of the priestly or Levitical classes. For families meeting these criteria, the ritual is an important one.

The payment to the kohen traditionally consists of five silver coins, though in modern times this is a monetary equivalent. The father presents the child to the kohen, asking whether he will redeem the boy for the prescribed amount. The kohen accepts the redemption and blesses the family. The kohen may then keep the payment or donate it, as he chooses.

The rite symbolizes a historical moment described in the Torah: the moment when God redeemed the Israelites' firstborn sons in Egypt before the Exodus. By performing pidyon haben, families connect themselves to that ancient deliverance and acknowledge God's power in their own lives through the birth of their son.

A festive meal accompanies the ceremony, often more elaborate than the brit milah, emphasizing its joyous redemptive nature. This celebration brings family and community together to mark the occasion.

In modern practice, some families hold pidyon haben even when the technical obligation is unclear—for instance, if a child's genealogy is uncertain—to maintain the tradition and its educational value. The ceremony serves both as a legal obligation under Jewish law and as a meaningful family celebration that connects the child to Jewish history and tradition.
